blurb: A young printer in Philadelphia makes a bold plan: to practise thirteen virtues, one week at a time, and track every slip in a little book.
source: Text: from The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, chapter IX “Plan for Attaining Moral Perfection”, Standard Ebooks edition, split into three parts. Public domain.

streets.name: The Printing Shop
streets.blurb: In his printing shop, Franklin plans a bold project: to live without any fault at all. First he writes his list of virtues.
streets.how: Set each virtue in type, letter by letter, before the ink dries.

params.done: Thirteen virtues, each with a short rule. Now for the plan.

streets.name: The 13 Virtues
streets.blurb: Franklin will practise one virtue a week, in order — Temperance first, because a clear head makes the rest easier.
streets.how: Pick up each virtue and put it on the chart in Franklin’s order, one per week.

params.objective: Put the first six virtues on the chart in order
params.hint: Temperance comes first. Look again at Franklin’s list.
params.done: One virtue a week — thirteen weeks for a whole course, four courses in a year.

streets.name: The Little Book
streets.blurb: Years later, Franklin looks back at his little book of black spots. Did the plan work?
streets.how: Read the pages of Franklin’s little book, then work out which virtue gave him the most trouble.

clues.label: The little book
clues.text: Red lines for the virtues, a column for each day — and a black spot for every fault. He was surprised how many there were.

clues.label: The messy desk
clues.text: Papers everywhere. As a busy master printer, people came to see him at their own hours, not his.

clues.label: The speckled ax
clues.text: A man wanted his whole ax ground bright — then gave up and said he liked a speckled ax best.

solve.label: The answer
solve.prompt: Which virtue gave Franklin the most trouble?
solve.hint: Think about the messy desk and the busy shop.

skyRun.name: Franklin’s Kite
skyRun.blurb: up past Franklin’s kite to the storm clouds above Philadelphia.
skyRun.how: Climb the rooftops and chimneys up to the storm clouds where Franklin’s kite is flying. Some ledges move — wait for them!

params.objective: Reach the kite in the clouds

npcs.name: Benjamin Franklin
npcs.idle: Lose no time; be always employed in something useful.
npcs.thanks: Every paper delivered on time. That is Industry!

steps.text: Talk to Benjamin Franklin outside his printing shop.
steps.say: The newspapers are printed, but my apprentice is late! Three bundles have blown off the cart. Could you find them and deliver them?

items.name: A newspaper for the coffee house
A newspaper for the post office

steps.text: Find the three bundles of newspapers.
Deliver the papers: coffee house, library and post office.

steps.say: Splendid. Early to bed and early to rise — and early with the papers!

vault.name: The Virtue Chart
vault.blurb: an escape room in Franklin’s study: build your own 13-week chart and compare it with Atomic Habits.
vault.intro: Franklin’s study. His little book lies open on the desk. Open three locks to build your own plan — and see what Franklin and Atomic Habits agree on.

stations.label: Your chart
stations.text: Put the steps of a 13-week virtue chart in order.
stations.lesson: One thing at a time, checked every day — that is how Franklin built habits.

items: Choose your virtues and write a short rule for each
Rule a page: a column for each day, a line for each virtue
Focus on just one virtue this week
Each evening, mark a spot for any slip
Next week, add the next virtue
solve.hint: Start by choosing, end by moving on.

stations.label: Franklin and Atomic Habits
stations.text: Match each part of Franklin’s plan to the Atomic Habits idea that is most like it (in our own words).
stations.lesson: Two hundred years apart, both say: make it small, make it visible, and keep going.

pairs: Start small: one habit at a time
Black spots in the little book
Track your habit so you can see it
Morning: what good shall I do today?
Decide when and where you will do it
A better and a happier man, though not perfect
Small improvements add up over time
solve.hint: Think about what each one is for.

quiz.label: Franklin’s clock
quiz.lesson: Franklin never became perfect — but the plan made him better and happier.

vault.openText: The study door opens onto a bright Philadelphia morning.
vault.outro: Franklin carried his little book all his life. Now you have a chart of your own.

badges.name: Habit Historian
badges.desc: Finish Franklin’s 13 virtues and Atomic Habits.
